newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Government camp looks strong ahead of Algeria poll.
newsitem.headline: Government camp looks strong ahead of Algeria poll.

text.p: The political camp supporting the Algerian government against that of the radical Islamists has staked out a strong position ahead of June 5 parliamentary elections, Algiers-based analysts say.
Fallout from more than five years of conflict has heavily tilted the power struggle in favour of government supporters to put them in a position to lead the June ballot, they say.

But few see the vote bringing a decisive end to the violence that erupted shortly after January 1992 when the authorities cancelled an election in which the radical Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) had taken a commanding lead.

Since then about 60,000 people have been killed including many civilians -- babies, young girls, the elderly -- slaughtered by having their throats cut, being beheaded, shot or blasted apart by bombs.

"The country has experienced unprecedented violence each day for more than five years between guerrillas and the government. This polarisation has forged a pro-government camp with strong support, mostly in the countryside," said one leading political analyst.
In a vast country of 29 million people where opinion polls are extremely rare, it is impossible to give firm breakdowns.
But in broad consensus, analysts say that about 40 percent of those who sympathised with radical Islamists in 1992 and 1993 appear to have switched their mood.

Many people felt they had become hostage to both the fundamentalist rebel "terror" and a government "repression" policy and would go along with what they saw as the best hope for a multi-party parliament to foster democracy.
This tended to favour pro-government parties like the National Democratic Rally led by President Liamine Zeroual's ally, Abdelkader Bensalah, whose views received more exposure.

Main opposition leaders, busy plotting strategies for the 380-seat National Assembly elections in June, accuse the government of limiting their parties from developing political activities through state control of the media and an emergency law in place since February 1992.
Rebel killings and the ousting by the government early in the conflict of elected FIS local councils have drained strength from the radical Islamist camp.
This allowed government supporters to dominate large sections of society in the absence of a credible opposition, still confined to some large cities, one analyst said.
About 60 percent of the people appeared to support the government through various social and political groups, with well-rooted influence mostly in the countryside, analysts said.

"Most of the voters are in the countryside where government local authorities still enjoy strong influence through local personalities and associations," said one analyst, who said he had travelled across much of Algeria to try to gauge trends.
Analysts see the elections, preceded by political reforms, as the conclusion of Zeroual's drive to carve out a political system from which radical Islamists are barred.
But Zeroual's view that the election will bring Algeria out of crisis is not shared by some politicians.

The legal opposition, some 60 political groups, has split into two main strands -- those opposing the FIS outright, and those who want the outlawed party's leaders included in negotiations to end the conflict, the analysts added.
The Socialist Forces Front (FFS), which came second to the FIS in the first round of the scrapped election five years ago, believes dialogue with the FIS is still essential.
So do many leading figures in the former sole ruling party, the now-divided National Liberation Front. But both will contest the poll.
"The authorities imposed on us the elections which continue a process started with the January 1992 coup d'etat," said one FFS leader, Seddik Debaili.
"The violence will continue with the elections, as well as the social crisis," Debaili said, but he added that the FFS had no choice but to contest the election or risk marginalisation.

"The legal opposition parties appear to be trapped by the change in a society struggling to heal its wounds, and politicians are forced again to jump into uncharted waters," said political analyst Abderrahame Balil.
Most analysts say an end to radical Islamism as a political focus of Algeria's bloody conflict remains to be seen.
Two legal Islamist parties, Hamas and Nahda, are competing for National Assembly seats.

"The elections will be a test case for the legal Islamists who have to prove that their representation in parliament will yield change, or risk losing credibility and then fuelling violent Islamists who advocate that change should only come through guns," said one analyst.
